Executive verdict
Overall assessment

The project is a substantial and credible major-project prototype. It already integrates three honeypots, centralized telemetry, multiple ML approaches, explainability, six analysis agents, analyst feedback, simulated IPS actions, dashboards, and alert automation. It is not yet safe to describe as production-ready. The next release should prioritize security boundaries, measurable evidence, frontend correctness, and one consistent project story.

The best improvement strategy is not to add more algorithms immediately. First make the existing system trustworthy, reproducible, and easy to demonstrate. Then strengthen the ML evaluation and user experience. This sequencing protects the work already completed and produces clearer academic evidence.

3. P0 remediation: make the current system trustworthy
3.1 Network exposure and secrets

The honeypot launcher defaults SSH, FTP, and HTTP to 0.0.0.0, and the Node server does not provide an explicit host to app.listen. This is convenient for a lab but unsafe as a default. The secure default should be loopback-only; wider binding should require an explicit environment setting such as AUTHORIZED_LAB_MODE=true plus a displayed warning.
Add BIND_HOST=127.0.0.1 as the default for every service, including dashboards and collectors.
Fail closed when JWT_SECRET, Flask session secret, ingestion secret, or alert signing secret is missing, too short, or matches a known development value.
Store only .env.example in version control. Rotate any credentials ever included in ZIP handoffs, old workflows, screenshots, or guide packages.
Add a startup preflight that prints safe configuration status without printing secret values.
3.2 Separate operational authentication from decoy capture

Captured credentials are valid research telemetry inside explicit honeypot services, but the analyst/admin portal is an operational system. Its real login password must never be copied into event payloads or logs. OWASP recommends excluding authentication passwords, access tokens, and session identifiers from application logs [S1].
At the portal boundary, retain username, result, timestamp, source class, request ID, and coarse client metadata; replace the password with a fixed redaction marker before any logger call.
Keep credential capture only in clearly named decoy modules and label those fields as sensitive research data.
Add automated tests that submit a unique canary password and assert that it does not appear in JSONL, SQLite, backend logs, webhook payloads, UI state, or test artifacts.
3.3 Authenticate and validate ingestion

POST /api/events and POST /api/ids-results currently accept data without an independent service credential. Login protection does not protect machine-to-machine ingestion. Use a separate trust boundary as recommended for protected REST endpoints [S2].
Sign each ingestion request with HMAC-SHA256 over a canonical body, timestamp, and nonce; or use a long scoped API key over TLS in a contained lab.
Reject timestamps outside a narrow window and repeated nonces. Rate-limit by credential and source address; return 429 with retry guidance.
Validate an explicit JSON schema, cap body size, reject unknown or overlong fields, and store a validation failure counter.
Never reuse the analyst JWT as the collector credential. Rotate independently and assign only the exact ingestion permission.
3.4 Make dashboard data honest

The backend currently generates two dashboard KPI values with Math.random(). This is a critical credibility fault. Replace them with deterministic queries and display data freshness. A missing metric should show “Unavailable” rather than a plausible random number.
Define every KPI formally: source table, filter, time window, aggregation, timezone, and refresh interval.
Return generated_at, data_from, data_to, and model_version with dashboard responses.
Add snapshot tests that seed a known database and assert exact KPI values.
3.5 Canonical alert path

Remove the frontend’s hard-coded localhost n8n URL and the older XAI webhook action. The browser should never send sensitive alert fields directly to an automation service. The server should generate one sanitized, schema-versioned alert and submit it through the existing canonical integration path.
Export the final n8n workflow into version control with no credentials, pin the n8n version, and add an import-and-smoke-test guide.
Use a single contract: event ID, time, service, coarse source, threat score, severity, model votes, redacted evidence summary, explanation summary, and dashboard deep link.
Record delivery status, response code, attempts, next retry, and dead-letter reason without storing secret webhook values.

5. Data, ML, and XAI improvement plan
5.1 Treat perfect accuracy as a question

The 100% LSTM result may be correct for the current held-out synthetic split, but it is not sufficient evidence of generalization. A balanced synthetic dataset can contain repeated templates, generator-specific wording, shared campaign patterns, or sequences that cross the train/test boundary. The final evaluation must separate related groups. GroupKFold is designed so the same group does not appear in both training and test sets [S3].
5.2 Evaluation design
Assign group IDs before splitting: campaign/session, source generator seed, payload family, or attack script. Preserve those IDs only for evaluation, not as predictive features.
Canonicalize and deduplicate payloads. Report exact and near-duplicate rates before and after splitting.
Create train, validation, and final test sets. Tune thresholds and hyperparameters only on validation; open the final test once for the report.
Run a temporal backtest and an out-of-generator test using newly produced scenarios that did not create the training set.
Add a small external or manually curated challenge set with clear licensing and provenance. Do not silently mix external data into the main synthetic result.

Repeat training across several seeds. Report mean, standard deviation, confidence intervals, confusion matrices, per-class precision/recall/F1, macro F1, balanced accuracy, false-positive rate, calibration and latency.
Run leakage tests: label shuffling, feature ablation, duplicate-group removal, and a simple lexical baseline. Suspiciously high performance after these checks should trigger dataset inspection.

5.4 Model governance

Use the NIST AI Risk Management Framework as a lightweight structure: govern the process, map the context, measure performance and risk, and manage changes [S5]. For this project, that means reproducible manifests rather than heavy bureaucracy.
Dataset card: origin, generator, labels, balance, sanitization, exclusions, known limitations, privacy and license/provenance.
Model card: intended lab use, prohibited use, training generation, features, thresholds, metrics, slice results, limitations and ethical boundaries.
Immutable candidate manifest: code commit, environment lock, data hashes, feature schema hash, random seeds, training config, model hashes and evaluation output.
Human promotion gate: no candidate becomes active without passing fixed tests and recording the approver and reason. Keep a tested rollback to the previous active version.
Drift signals: feature missingness/range, attack distribution, prediction distribution, confidence, disagreement, feedback corrections, false positives and latency.
6. Reliability, storage, automation, and agents
6.1 Durable event pipeline

The current JSONL fallback is useful, but silent queue drops and infinite per-record retry can hide loss or block later records. Convert the asynchronous collector path into an observable, bounded pipeline.
Persist outgoing records to a local outbox before delivery; acknowledge/delete only after the destination commits.
Use exponential backoff with a maximum attempt count, then move the record to a dead-letter store with the last error.
Expose queue depth, oldest age, total dropped, retry count, dead-letter count and destination status on the health page.
Use idempotency keys so retried events do not create duplicate incidents.
6.2 SQLite and logs
SQLite is suitable for this single-machine lab when configured deliberately. WAL mode permits readers and writers to proceed concurrently in common cases [S6].
Enable WAL and a sensible busy_timeout; validate behavior under concurrent API/dashboard writes.
Add schema versioning/migrations and indexes for timestamp, severity, attack type, service, event ID and feedback status.
Paginate and filter queries in SQL; do not read and split the complete JSONL file for routine dashboard requests.
Rotate JSONL by date/size, compress closed segments, define retention, and verify backup/restore from a clean directory.
Keep an append-only audit trail for feedback, alert retries, model promotion and simulated IPS decisions.
6.3 Agent orchestration
Define a versioned input/output schema for each of the six agents; reject invalid output and record schema version.
Set per-agent timeout and total incident budget. One failed agent must not block the complete dashboard result.
Record started/completed/failed/timeout, duration, error class and evidence references. Show partial completion honestly.
Use circuit breakers for repeatedly failing integrations and allow a safe retry from the incident page.
Treat ATT&CK mappings as evidence-linked hypotheses. Do not show a technique ID unless a rule or observable supports it.

9.1 Security acceptance
All services are loopback-only unless an explicit authorized-lab configuration is enabled.
Startup fails for missing/default secrets; repository and release secret scans are clean.
A unique real-portal password never appears in any log, database event, webhook payload, UI state, test report, screenshot, or exported bundle.
Unauthenticated, expired, replayed, oversized and schema-invalid ingestion requests are rejected and counted.
Role and session tests cover login throttling, logout, expiry, privilege checks and CSRF strategy.
File download tests cover encoded traversal, mixed separators, absolute paths and unexpected extensions.
9.2 Functional and reliability acceptance
A controlled attack scenario appears in JSONL/SQLite, IDS result, XAI, agent output, dashboard, alert and audit trail with one consistent event ID.
Stopping the collector or n8n does not silently lose accepted events; retry/dead-letter status is visible and recovery is idempotent.
Every dashboard KPI equals a known seeded database query; no random or placeholder metric is displayed as operational truth.
Backup/restore, artifact integrity, schema migration and rollback pass from a clean temporary directory.
Graceful shutdown flushes pending work and releases the required ports.
9.3 ML/XAI acceptance
Train/validation/test groups are disjoint and split manifests are hashed.
Results include per-class and aggregate metrics, confidence intervals or multi-seed variation, calibration, latency and the exact decision thresholds.
Challenge events generated after the split definition are evaluated separately and not used for tuning.
Each explanation names the component being explained and never implies SHAP explains the complete hybrid decision unless it actually does.
Model candidate promotion and rollback are human-approved, auditable and reproducible.

Methodology: distinguish supervised multiclass classification, unsupervised anomaly detection, sequence classification, scoring, explanation and agent enrichment.
Results: include per-class metrics, false positives, latency, confusion matrices, generalization tests, limitations and failed/weak components—not only best accuracy.
Slides: use real dashboard screenshots, one end-to-end event trace, one explanation, one failure/retry example, and one ethics/scope slide.
Viva preparation: create a claim-to-evidence table so each answer points to a code file, artifact hash, test, metric, screenshot or reproducible command.

Run startup preflight and show all services healthy on loopback.
Generate one known SSH/FTP/HTTP attack scenario in the authorized lab.
Trace the same event ID through telemetry, normalized storage, detector votes, hybrid score, SHAP explanation, agent enrichment and dashboard.
Show a sanitized alert, then intentionally stop n8n and demonstrate visible retry/dead-letter behavior without data loss.

Bottom line

The project already contains enough technical breadth. Its strongest path to a higher-quality final submission is disciplined consolidation: secure the boundaries, make every number real, validate generalization, build one excellent dashboard, and make the documents tell exactly the same story as the code.
